Investigation Lab — rdp-lateral-001
  1 / 1
Start●

An alert fired overnight. Decide whether it is real.

no experience needed

Your security tool fired this alert at 03:04:

The alertSuspicious authentication activity - RDP lateral movement Severity: HIGH A single internal account produced successful logons on multiple internal servers, chained together by RDP connections (TCP 3389) between those servers.

Your job is to answer one question and be able to defend it: is this a real attack that must be escalated, or a false alarm that can be closed?

You will answer it the way a real analyst does — not by guessing, but by following the evidence from the first search to the last, and writing down what you find as you go. By the last card you will know which account moved, which servers it reached, how it travelled between them, when, and what a reviewer should do about it.

What this guide is

It starts at zeroNo security knowledge, no Elastic experience, no typing. If you can double-click a file, you can do this lab.
It shows your real screenEvery picture in here is a screenshot of this exact lab, taken from the running product, with numbered circles on the control to use.
It never leaves you guessingEvery step says what to type, what number to expect, and what it proves.
It cleans up after itselfOne file starts the lab. One file removes it completely. Nothing is left behind.

How to move around

This guide is a deck of cards, one step each. Move through it however you like:

  • The Next and Back buttons at the bottom, or the arrow keys on your keyboard.
  • The row of pills under the header jumps you straight to any step.
  • On a phone, swipe left and right.
  • Press ? any time for help, or the printer icon top right to save the whole guide as a PDF.
Two honest notes, read them before you start

1. The screen pictures contain the answers. That is deliberate. Use them the way a navigator uses a map: hold yours next to them, and if the words and numbers match you are in the right place with the right query. But the thing being assessed is the report you write — your reasoning, your timeline, your verdict. Copying a screenshot into a report is not investigating, and it is the easiest way to fail this.

2. Kibana prints clock times in your timezone, not UTC. Every log in this lab is stored in UTC. If your machine is not set to UTC, every time you see will be shifted by your UTC offset. Card 7 explains exactly what to do about it, and why it does not affect your conclusion.

The coloured markings, used throughout

Yellow marks a value you have to read off your own screen and record in your report — it is the blank. Green marks a value or a sentence the guide is handing you outright: it appears in the Finding boxes from card 12 onwards, and in the figures you fill in on the last two cards. Before card 12 there are no green answers — up to that point every value you need is either on your screen or in a screenshot.

The one thing you need first

Docker Desktop, installed and running. That is the only prerequisite. The lab runs inside it and installs nothing else on your computer. If you do not have Docker Desktop yet, ask your instructor — this lab assumes it is already there.

Prep1

The words you need to know

read once

You will see all of these in the tool and in your report. Read them once now and the rest of the lab becomes much easier.

The pieces

AlertA rule that fires when something looks dangerous. It is a hint, not a fact. It might be nothing at all.
ElasticsearchThe database that stores and searches the logs. Answers web addresses like localhost:9200.
KibanaThe website you do all the work in, sitting on top of Elasticsearch. Lives at localhost:5601.
IndexOne named pile of log records of the same shape. Ours are auth-2026.09.22 and network-2026.09.22.
Data viewKibana’s word for “which pile shall I look at”. Older versions called it an index pattern.
DocumentOne single log record. There are 294 in the auth pile and 126 in network.
FieldOne labelled box inside a document, like source.ip. The part before the dot is the group.
TimestampThe @timestamp field — when it happened. All times in this lab are stored in UTC.
QueryA typed question, like “show me events where the code is 4625”.
KQLThe query language Kibana speaks. The ? button in the search bar explains it.
RDPRemote Desktop Protocol — logging in to another Windows machine’s desktop over the network. Always TCP port 3389.
Lateral movementAn attacker who has broken into one machine hopping over to a different machine, still inside your network.

The two verdicts you will have to choose between

True positiveThe attack is real. Escalate it, contain it, tell someone.
False positiveNothing bad happened. Close the alert with a note saying why not.

The event codes you will meet

Windows records everything as a numbered event code. Three of them matter here. The lab’s data view already knows which is which, so you never have to memorise them — but you do have to be able to say what each one means:

CodeMeaningDoes it help you here?
4624An account was successfully logged onYes — this is the whole alert
4625An account failed to log onNo — a deliberate dead end, see card 9
4740An account was locked outNo — more of the same noise

The fields this investigation runs on

Almost every question here is answered by a handful of fields. Learn these and you can read the raw logs as well as the screen:

FieldReads likeThe question it answers
event.code4624, 4625, 4740What kind of event was this?
event.outcomesuccess, failureDid it work?
user.namerneuman, jdoeWhich account?
host.namesec-win-03Which machine did it land on?
host.ip10.0.4.11What is that machine’s address?
source.ip10.0.4.11Where did it come from?
destination.ip10.0.4.12Where did the connection go?
destination.port3389What kind of connection was it?
network.protocolrdp, smb, dnsWhich protocol carried it?

Read host.ip and source.ip carefully — they look alike and they are the two halves of this whole case. One is where the event happened, the other is where it came from. Card 13 is built entirely on the difference between them.

One word you will see in a confusing place

Document count. The number in the Documents tab is how many log records matched your query. It is not the number of machines, accounts or events. Three documents can be three machines, or three attempts on one machine. Every finding in this lab is about turning a count into a list you can read.

Start the lab with one file

first run is slowthen wait

The lab is a real Elastic Stack running on your own computer, hidden behind one file that does all the work. You start it once; it loads everything for you. There is a Windows file and a Linux / macOS file, and they are twins — the same steps in the same order, so either platform gives you the identical lab.

Do this

  1. Open the lab folder — the folder that contains this guide.
  2. On Windows: find setup-lab.cmd and double-click it. On macOS or Linux: open a terminal in this folder and run chmod +x setup-lab.sh once, then ./setup-lab.sh.
  3. A black window (or a terminal) opens and starts downloading Elasticsearch and Kibana. Do not close it.
  4. Wait until it prints The lab is ready. and the two addresses. This is the slow part: 5 to 20 minutes the very first time, seconds afterwards.

The one thing that stops most people

Docker must be installed and running. The lab runs both programs inside Docker containers — it installs nothing else on your computer. If the setup file says docker was not found, or that it is installed but the engine is not responding, start Docker, wait until it says Engine running, and run the file again. That one check fixes almost every startup problem.

What you should see

A window that works through numbered stages, ending with:

The last thing the setup file prints ============================================================== The lab is ready. Elasticsearch : http://127.0.0.1:9200 Kibana : http://127.0.0.1:5601 data view "auth" index pattern auth-* data view "network" index pattern network-* ... Kibana login lab_kibana / LabKibana001 ... The rule that fired Security -> Alerts 3 alerts

What it did for you while you waited

So the output does not frighten you, the script performed exactly the five jobs that would otherwise be the hard part of this lab:

  • Started two programs — Elasticsearch (the database) and Kibana (the website).
  • Taught Elasticsearch what each field means. An index template declares “source.ip holds a network address” before any data arrives. Without it Elasticsearch guesses, and guessing quietly breaks your searches: a destination.port: 3389 filter can silently return nothing at all.
  • Loaded the log data, then re-read the document counts to prove the import landed — 294 and 126.
  • Created your two data views, then read the stored index pattern back to prove it was not empty. A data view with an empty pattern matches nothing, and Discover then shows zero fields with no visible reason why.
  • Installed the detection rule and waited for it to fire, so the Alerts page is not empty when you arrive. Without a fired rule that page renders nothing at all, and the next card would be a dead end.

Two credentials, and one of them is the browser

The lab account

This lab’s stack has security switched on, because a detection rule cannot exist on a cluster with security off. That means two things to type, and they are the same two:

  • In the browser, on the sign-in screen: lab_kibana / LabKibana001
  • In a terminal, on any command you run by hand: curl -u lab_kibana:LabKibana001 …

They are throwaway lab credentials that protect nothing. The browser asks once and then remembers you.

The two data views waiting for you

Data viewMatches which indexHoldsDocuments
auth-*auth-2026.09.22Logons, logoffs, failures, lockouts, Kerberos failures, privilege assignments, process starts294
network-*network-2026.09.22Connections between machines: SMB, RPC, DNS, LDAP, RDP, HTTP, SSH126

The * is a wildcard meaning “anything starting with auth”, so one entry covers every day of auth logs and you never have to pick a date-bearing index.

Already started it twice?

Completely safe. The script counts what is already there and skips the work, and it will not install a second copy of the detection rule either. Your data will not load twice — which matters, because duplicate documents would double every count in the rest of this guide and quietly ruin your findings. If it ever finds a half-loaded index it stops and tells you to run the setup file with reset instead of guessing.

Ports, if something else already owns one

Elasticsearch wants 9200 and Kibana wants 5601. If either is taken, the script refuses to touch a cluster it did not start and tells you which one is in the way. Change the ESPORT and KBPORT lines at the top of the setup file, then run it with regen-compose and it rewrites the compose file for you. You never have to edit that by hand.

The alertSuspicious authentication activity - RDP lateral movement Severity: HIGH A single internal user account produced successful logons on multiple internal servers, chained together by RDP connections (TCP 3389) between those servers.
If you get a sign-in screen instead

This lab’s Kibana has security switched on, so it asks who you are once. The account is lab_kibana and the password is LabKibana001. They are throwaway lab credentials that protect nothing. Sign in and carry on; the browser remembers you for the rest of the lab.

What is on the page

  • Just above the table, next to Columns, a count of 3 alerts. Not one summary line: three separate alerts, one per matching log record.
  • A Severity column reading high on every row, with a Risk Score of 73 beside it. The rule graded this as serious but not catastrophic.
  • A Reason column on each row, naming the fields that matched. Every one of them is drawn for the account rneuman.
  • A Status column reading Open (stored as active). Nothing has been closed yet; that is your job.

Do this

  1. Read the Severity and Risk Score columns and write both down.
  2. Read the alert count just above the table. Write the number down — you will check it against your own query later, and the two have to agree.
  3. Read the Reason column on any row. Write down which fields it names and which account it is drawn for.
  4. Open one alert. In the first column, called Actions, click the first small icon — the two arrows pointing outwards. A panel opens showing that one alert.
  5. In that panel, read Alert reason and Highlighted fields. Then click the Table tab at the top of the panel: that is the raw log record underneath, with its event.code, host.name and source.ip.
Two different times, and the difference matters

The alert’s own timestamp is when the rule ran — a minute or two ago, because the rule is still running every minute. The log record underneath it happened on 22 September, mid-morning UTC, which is when the attack was. So the alerts are new and the events they point at are old, and the alerts page will keep showing them while Discover — which looks at the events themselves — shows you nothing at all until you set its time range. That is card 6, and it is not a fault.

You are not imagining it, and nothing has gone wrong. Open one alert on the JSON tab and you will find two clocks on it:

The two timestamps, from one alert@timestamp 2026-09-29T06:24:19.481Z the day YOU ran this kibana.alert.original_time 2026-09-22T10:00:00.000Z the morning of the attack

@timestamp is when Elastic noticed. It is the day you ran the setup file, so it is a different date for every batch and it tells you nothing about the attack. kibana.alert.original_time is when the activity actually happened, and that one never moves — for this lab it is always 22 September. So: an alert is a claim that something happened; the original time is the evidence for it. Every real SOC works this way, because logs often arrive late or a rule is run against history, and if alerts were dated by the event, today’s real alerts would be buried under a wall of old ones.

Which one goes in your report? The original time. Every time you write in this lab, write the time of the activity, never the time the tool noticed it.

The rule that fired

Worth seeing, because the rule and your own investigation are the same filter.

  1. Open the hamburger menu (☰) in the top left, then Security → Rules. That is the page of detection rules; ours is the only one you have, so it sits under Custom rules. Older builds call the page Detection rules.
  2. Open the rule called One internal account logging on to several internal servers in quick succession.
  3. Read its query. It is the filter you will type by hand on card 10 — character for character.
The rule's own query, and the account it namesevent.code: 4624 and event.outcome: "success" and user.name: "rneuman"
Why this is worth two minutes

Because it means the alert count and your query count have to agree. The rule says 3, so when the query on card 10 later returns 3 you have not merely found the same answer twice — you have found the same answer the monitoring system found, by a different road. If the two numbers ever disagree, one of them is wrong, and now you know which one to trust.

The rule also tells you which three fields matter, and they are the three this whole investigation turns on: the event code, the outcome, and the account. Everything else — which server, from where, how it travelled — is yours to work out.

If the table is empty, it is the time picker

Not a broken lab. An alert is stamped with the time it was raised, so the range this page starts on — Today, meaning from midnight — stops covering it once you cross midnight. Click the time picker at the top right, switch to the Relative tab, and set it to 1 unit Days. Some versions put a ready-made Last 24 hours button there instead, which does the same job. The three alerts come straight back. The lab itself never changed.

What you should have now

One rule, three high-severity alerts, risk score 73, all raised against successful logons for the account rneuman. You have not run a single query yet and you already know the shape of the case: one account, several internal servers, and an attacker who is inside your network rather than outside it. Three questions remain, and they are the rest of this guide: how many servers, which ones, and how it moved between them.

Here is the screen before you click, exactly as it appears:

And after you click it

And the three groups in the field list on the left

Once the range is right, the sidebar fills in and shows three named groups. Learn the three names now, because you will click inside them repeatedly:

GroupWhat is in itWhat you do with it
Available fieldsThe 15 fields this data view can search: @timestamp, event.*, host.ip, host.name, message, process.name, process.parent.name, source.ip, source.port, user.domain, user.nameHover a row and click ⊕ to make it a column, or click the field name to open its Top values panel

The network-* pile has 16 fields and three different names — destination.ip, destination.port, network.protocol and network.bytes. You will meet those on card 15.

So what was wrong?

Exactly one thing: the time range. The data view is right, the search bar is right, Kibana is healthy. The logs are simply older than the last fifteen minutes.

That is the single most common reason a beginner meets an empty screen. Learn the reflex now and it will serve you for years: an empty screen is a time-range problem or a data-view problem, nine times out of ten. It is almost never the query.

One button on this screen you must not press

Next to Save, in the top bar, there is a blue Try ES|QL button. ES|QL is a different query language, and this guide only ever uses the KQL box in the search bar. If you press it, the search bar is replaced by this:

The query box now reads FROM auth-* | LIMIT 10 instead of your KQL, and the panel above it says ES|QL help. Nothing is broken — the button that used to say Try ES|QL now says Switch to classic, and pressing that gets you back. Or simply press the browser’s Back button. You do not need ES|QL for this lab, and you will not be asked about it.

Pick a pile5

There are three data views. One of them is a trap.

which logs?2 min

Before you type a single query, be able to say which pile you are reading. Open the dropdown on the far left of the search bar — the control with the label Data view beside it.

So why does the dropdown show three when the lab made two?

What each pile holds

Data viewDocumentsWhat is insideUsed on
auth-*294Logons (4624), logoffs (4634), failures (4625), lockouts (4740), Kerberos failures (4771), privilege assignments (4672), process starts (4688)Cards 8–14
network-*126Connections between machines: DNS 26, SMB 19, RPC 16, ICMP 15, HTTP 14, SSH 12, LDAP 12, HTTPS 10, and RDP 2Cards 15–17

Hold on to that last number. There are exactly two RDP connections in the entire network pile, and the whole investigation turns on them.

Why a data view matters at all

A data view is a bookmark. It tells Kibana which pile of documents to read and which field holds the time. Pick the wrong one and a perfectly good query returns nothing at all, because the documents it is looking for are not in that pile.

So whenever a query returns zero results, check these three things in this order: the data view, then the time range, then the query itself. Fix them in that order and you will never waste time debugging a query that was never broken.

One quirk to expect, so it does not alarm you

The columns you choose stay chosen when you switch data views. When you go to network-* on card 15 your table will still be showing host.name, source.ip and host.ip from the auth pile. That is normal, it is not a bug, and card 16 simply adds three more columns to what is already there.

Be precise6

Your time range, and the one trap in this whole lab

read this one twice4 min

Right now your range reads Sep 22, 2026 @ 08:04:34.437 → Sep 22, 2026 @ 17:59:07.708. Kibana worked that out for you when you pressed Search entire time range, and it is exactly right: it is the first and last log record in the lab. Leave it there and carry on. You do not need to change anything to finish this investigation.

The trap: Kibana prints times in your timezone

Every timestamp in this lab is stored in UTC. The two numbers above are UTC. But the @timestamp column, the histogram axis, and the friendly dates inside a document all follow your computer’s timezone, and no setting anywhere in Kibana changes that. If your machine is 8 hours ahead of UTC, the logon this guide calls 10:00:00.000 appears in your table as 18:00:00.000, and the range buttons read 16:04:34.437 and Sep 23, 01:59:07.708.

So which is right? Both, and it does not matter. Here is the rule that keeps you out of trouble:

  • Read the clock times off your own screen and write down what you see. Your timeline will be internally consistent, which is all a timeline needs to be.
  • Trust the gaps, never the absolute numbers. Every conclusion in this guide is about how far apart things are, and a timezone shift moves every time by exactly the same amount. The gaps here — 7 minutes, then 9 — are identical on every machine on earth.
  • Quote times as UTC in your report if you want to be unambiguous, and add one line saying they were read from a Kibana screen in your local timezone.
  • Want the screen to match the pictures in this guide exactly? Set your computer’s timezone to UTC before you start. Not required — but then nothing on the following cards will look out of place.

If you would rather pin the window yourself

Worth learning, because pinning a window is what you do on a real job. Click the left-hand of the two time buttons — the one reading Sep 22, 2026 @ 08:04:34.4…. This panel opens:

Three days wide is deliberate. Sep 21 00:00 → Sep 24 00:00 is comfortably wider than the data, so it still contains all 294 documents no matter where in the world your computer is — a one-day window typed in local dates can silently clip the tail off the data if you are east of UTC.

One more trap: the range resets itself

If you press F5 to reload, or wander off to another page and come back, the time range can snap back to Last 15 minutes and the screen goes empty again with the blue Search entire time range button back in the middle. That is not your fault and nothing is broken — just click the button again. Some analysts keep the working Discover tab open in a bookmark for exactly this reason.

Investigate7

Query 1 — every successful logon, as a baseline

1 of 7 queries2 min
Goal of this step

Get one number you can trust before you chase anything. An analyst who starts from a specific suspicion has already decided what to find. Start from the population, then narrow.

Do this

  1. Click in the search bar. The grey hint Filter your data using KQL syntax disappears.
  2. Type the query below, exactly — including the double quotes.
  3. Press Enter.
Query 1 — data view auth-* event.code: 4624 and event.outcome: "success"

What you should see

What 72 actually tells you

Seventy-two successful logons happened on this fleet yesterday. They were made by six different accounts, spread over six machines, spread evenly through the day. None of that is an attack. It is the background.

Write this number down. It is your control: whenever a later number looks alarming, you can say exactly how much of it is ordinary.

Reading the query

Three clauses, joined by the word and. Every one of them is a filter, and the only one doing any real work is the first:

ClauseReads asEffect
event.code: 4624the event code is the number 4624Keeps only successful logons — 72 of 294
event.outcome: "success"the outcome is the word successNothing — every 4624 already succeeded. Keeping it makes the intent explicit and protects you if the data ever changes.
Numbers get quotes, words do not — and getting it wrong fails silently

event.code: 4624 works because event.code is a number. event.outcome: "success" needs the quotes because event.outcome is text. Drop the quotes and you do not get an error — you get zero results and no explanation. The little icons in the left field list tell you which is which, and they are worth learning:

Icon in the field listMeansExample fieldWrite it as
#numberevent.codeevent.code: 4624
ksingle word / keyworduser.nameuser.name: "rneuman"
iIP addressdestination.ipsource.ip: "10.0.4.11"
tfree textmessagerarely filter on it
🕑date and time@timestamp@timestamp > "2026-09-22"

Safest habit of all: always quote the value, number or not. user.name: 'rneuman' and event.code: '4624' both work in KQL, and neither can surprise you.

Next

The alert is about one account hopping between servers. The obvious next move is to go hunting for the account. Do not do that yet. First spend one minute on the other kind of login event — the failures. It is the single most common place an investigation goes to die, and you are about to see why.

Investigate8

Query 2 — the failures. This is a dead end.

2 of 7 queriesa trap, on purpose
Goal of this step

Rule out the boring explanation. An account logging on to several servers in minutes could be somebody fat-fingering their password on the wrong keyboard, and failed logons are what a bad password looks like. It takes one minute to rule that out, and ruling it out is worth far more than the minute cost.

Do this

  1. Select the text in the search bar and replace it with the query below.
  2. Press Enter.
  3. Then click user.name in the field list on the left, near the bottom. A small panel opens showing the top values for that field. That panel is the whole point of this card — do not skip it.
Query 2 — data view auth-* event.code: 4625

What you should see

Dead end. Here is why, in one sentence

41 failed logons is a scary number that proves nothing — they belong to five different accounts, spread almost evenly, from four different external addresses, and the alerted account rneuman does not appear once.

There is more of the same in this pile, in case you were tempted to go further: 30 lockouts (event.code: 4740) and 22 Kerberos failures (event.code: 4771), also spread across the same five accounts. None of it touches rneuman. Try it if you like; it will not change the conclusion, and that is a useful thing to learn about yourself.

Why this card exists, and why it is early

Because a plausible dead end visited early is worth more than a success found later. You have now personally established that password guessing is not the story here, and it cost ninety seconds. An analyst who skips this step spends an hour proving the same thing badly, because 41 is a number that feels like a finding.

Put differently: 41 failures from five accounts is background noise; 3 successes on three different machines is a story. Volume is not significance. Learn to feel that difference and you will be a much better analyst than most people who have been doing this for years.

A habit worth forming here

When a count surprises you, do not stop at the count. Click the field and look at the distribution. “41” means nothing on its own. “41 spread across five accounts, none of them the one in the alert” means everything. The Top values panel costs one click and is the single most under-used tool in Kibana.

Next

Now the alert has told you which account to look at. Go and pull every successful logon for it. This is the step where the case opens up.

Investigate9

Query 3 — every successful logon for the alerted account

3 of 7 queriesthe breakthrough
Goal of this step

Take the population from card 8 and cut it down to the one account in the alert. Three filters, and the answer is three records.

Do this

  1. Replace the search bar contents with the query below and press Enter.
  2. Look at the tab. Then read the three rows, one at a time.
Query 3 — data view auth-*  ·  this is also the one-shot query from the alert brief user.name: "rneuman" and event.code: 4624 and event.outcome: "success"

What you should see

Read the three rows properly

Each row is one log record, and the wide Summary column contains all of its fields. Reading row 3, the oldest one:

FieldValue on the oldest rowPlain English
@timestampSep 22, 2026 @ 10:00:00.000When. (Add your UTC offset if your machine is not on UTC.)
event.code4,6244624. The comma is only a thousands separator — it is still the number 4624.
event.outcomesuccessIt worked. The credentials were valid.
user.namerneumanWhich account.
host.namesec-win-03Which machine it landed on.
host.ip10.0.4.11That machine’s address.
source.ip10.0.4.11Where it came from. On this first row, the same machine.
source.port40,000The local TCP port. The other two rows use 40,001 and 40,002 — read that as a sequence, not a coincidence.
event.actionuser_loginWindows calls it a user logon.
What you have established

One account, three successful logons, three different machines, inside sixteen minutes — on a day when the same fleet saw 72 logons spread evenly from morning to evening. That is a pattern, and no ordinary user behaves like that.

Write down the three timestamps now, in the order you read them, oldest first: 10:00:00.000, 10:07:00.137, 10:16:00.274. Read them off your screen and use your numbers if your timezone shifts them — but write down the gaps as well: 7 minutes, then 9. The gaps never change.

One quick check that costs nothing and is worth doing

Delete the two event clauses so the query reads only user.name: "rneuman", and press Enter. You still get 3.

That means this account did nothing at all on this fleet that day except these three logons — no failures, no lockouts, no process starts, nothing. A genuine staff account that had been let in and got confused would leave a mess. A clean, minimal, three-step path is what an operator leaves behind. Put that sentence in your report; it is the difference between describing a login and explaining one.

Next

You have three records and you have read one of them. Rather than squint at a Summary column, let Kibana tabulate all the fields for you at once — one screen, six separate claims proved.

Investigate10

One screen that proves six different things

do not skip this2 min
Goal of this step

Stop reading records one at a time. Get Kibana to summarise every field of your three records in a single table, with a distinct-value count for each.

Do this

  1. Leave the query exactly as it is on card 10.
  2. Click the Field statistics tab — the one immediately to the right of Documents ( 3 ). It is a tab, not a section further down the page.
Six claims, one screen, no scrolling through records
FieldDistinctWhat it proves
host.name3Three different servers, not one server three times
host.ip3And they are three different addresses, so they are three different machines
source.ip2Only two places the account came from — the key finding
event.code1All three are 4624: 1 value (4624). No other event type is hiding in here.
user.name1All three are the same account, as expected
source.port3Ports 40,000, 40,001, 40,002 — a consecutive run
@timestamp3Three different times, obviously
event.outcome1All three succeeded — already in the query, now confirmed
Do not misread the Documents (%) column

Every row says 3 (100%). That is not saying “these 3 documents are important”. It is saying “this field is present, with a value, in 3 of the 3 documents I matched”. A field that appears in every document tells you nothing on its own. Compare the Distinct values column against the document count — 3 out of 3 means three different things happened, and 1 out of 3 means the same thing happened three times.

Two ways back to the records, and both are on screen
  • Click the Documents ( 3 ) tab to the left to return to the rows.
  • Click the ▸ arrow at the left of a field-statistics row to expand that single field and see its actual values. Try it on host.name — it lists the three server names and how many logons each received.

Get into the habit of running every interesting query through this tab. It is fast, it is hard to misread, and it is the screen a reviewer will ask to see.

Next

You know there are three different servers. Name them. That means adding a column — and the ⊕ button that does it is one hover away.

Investigate11

Query 4 — name the three servers

4 of 7 queriesadd a column
Goal of this step

Turn “three different machines” into three names you can put in a report, with the time each one was reached.

Do this

  1. Go back to the Documents ( 3 ) tab. (The query is unchanged.)
  2. Find host.name in the field list on the left.
  3. Move the mouse over that row. A small ⊕ button appears at the far right of the row. Click it.

The ⊕ button is how you add a field as a column. If you do not see it, the mouse is not on the row — hover and look again. The same button removes a column, so if you press it twice you are back where you started.

What you should see

The finding, in the order you should read it

RowTime (UTC)ServerGap since the row above
3 (oldest)10:00:00.000sec-win-03— the first one
210:07:00.137sec-win-02+ 7 minutes
1 (newest)10:16:00.274sec-win-05+ 9 minutes

Kibana lists the newest record first, which is the opposite of the order you want in a timeline. Sort by @timestamp ascending, or just read the three rows bottom-up as above.

Write these down now, before you do anything else

Three server names in order: sec-win-03 → sec-win-02 → sec-win-05. Three times: 10:00:00.000, 10:07:00.137, 10:16:00.274. Gaps: 7 minutes, then 9.

And the sentence that will go in your report:

Finding 1A single internal account, rneuman, completed three successful logons on three different internal servers within a 16-minute window on 22 September 2026.
Is three servers in sixteen minutes actually suspicious?

Yes — but only in combination with two other things, and it is worth being able to say why.

  • The server names are not consecutive. sec-win-03, sec-win-02, sec-win-05 — whoever this was did not walk the numbering in order, which is what a well-meaning administrator or an inventory sweep would look like.
  • The account did nothing else. Three logons, no failures, no other activity at all. A person who fat-fingers a password leaves failures behind.
  • The logons succeeded. The credentials were valid, so this is not a guessing attack. Somebody is using a real account.

Any one of those on its own is a Tuesday. All three together is the alert. Two cards from now you will have the fourth.

Next

You know where the account landed. The interesting question is where each logon came from. Add two more columns.

Investigate12

Query 5 — where did each logon come from?

5 of 7 queriesthe key card
Goal of this step

Compare source.ip against host.ip, row by row. This is the single comparison the whole case rests on.

Do this

  1. The query is still the card 10 query. Leave it.
  2. Hover source.ip in the field list and click its ⊕ button.
  3. Hover host.ip and click its ⊕ button too.

Adding host.ip as well as source.ip is deliberate. One address on its own means nothing; the two side by side mean everything.

What you should see

Now compare them, oldest row first

TimeLanded on (host.ip)Came from (source.ip)What that means
10:00:00.00010.0.4.11  sec-win-0310.0.4.11Same machine. The logs do not say how the account first got here.
10:07:00.13710.0.4.12  sec-win-0210.0.4.11Came from sec-win-03 — the machine used one row earlier.
10:16:00.27410.0.4.13  sec-win-0510.0.4.12Came from sec-win-02 — the machine used two rows earlier.
This is the finding. Say it exactly.

Each logon came from the address of the machine the previous logon landed on. Not from the internet. Not from a different network. From 10.0.4.11, then 10.0.4.12 — the two machines the account had already reached.

Two consequences follow, and you need both in your report:

  • The attacker never came from outside. Every source.ip begins 10.0.4., so the account was already inside the network before this window started. This is a compromised internal account, not an outside attacker who got in during these sixteen minutes.
  • It is a chain, not three separate events. The three logons are not independent — each one is downstream of the last. That is what makes it lateral movement.
Finding 2 — put this in your report almost word for wordEach of the three logons originated from the internal address of the host reached by the previous logon (10.0.4.11 -> 10.0.4.12 -> 10.0.4.13). No external source address appears. This is a compromised internal account performing lateral movement inside 10.0.4.0/24, not an external intrusion.
What the data does not tell you — and what to write instead

The very first logon has source.ip equal to its own host.ip. That means this dataset does not contain the original compromise. Somebody was already on sec-win-03 before 10:00, and nothing in these two data views records how.

The professional move is to say so in the report rather than invent a story. Write a line like:

Write this in the Limitations sectionThe available telemetry begins at the first logon and does not cover the initial access. The mechanism by which the account was first authenticated on 10.0.4.11 is not evidenced in this data and requires host-based forensics on that machine to establish.

An analyst who marks the edge of their evidence is trusted. An analyst who quietly fills the gap with a guess is not, and one day it will be wrong in front of someone who matters.

The comparison is easy to get wrong on a tired afternoon

host.ip is the machine the event happened on. source.ip is where it came from. They read almost identically and they mean opposite things. Check which way round you are before you write the sentence — “the logon came from 10.0.4.11 to 10.0.4.12” is right; “the logon came from 10.0.4.12 to 10.0.4.11” is the same event said backwards, and it would turn your chain inside out.

Next

One more piece of evidence from the auth pile, then you switch to the other one: read a whole record, the way you would in a real investigation, so you can quote it.

Investigate13

Read one whole record

quote this in your report2 min
Goal of this step

See one event as a whole record rather than as a column. Every log has a message field written in plain English, and a sentence you can quote is worth more in a report than three field names.

Do this

  1. In the results table, click the small ⇅ button at the far left of any row — immediately left of the @timestamp column.
  2. A Document panel slides in from the right. That is the whole record.
Do not click the row

Clicking the row itself, or the timestamp, or the text in a field, does nothing at all — no error, no panel, just silence, and it is the single most common reason beginners think the tool is broken. The control is the tiny two-headed arrow ⇅ in its own narrow column to the left of the timestamp. It is small; look for it deliberately.

The field that goes straight into your report

Scroll the panel to message. For the record shown it reads:

The message field, verbatimAn account was successfully logged on. User: rneuman. Source Network Address: 10.0.4.12.

That is the same fact as event.code: 4624 + event.outcome: success + user.name: rneuman + source.ip: 10.0.4.12, written for a human. Quote it. A report line that reads “the log record states: ‘An account was successfully logged on. User: rneuman. Source Network Address: 10.0.4.12.’” is unimpeachable in a way that “source 10.0.4.12 per event.code 4624” is not.

Check the other two records while the panel is open

Click the ‹ arrow to step back through 1 of 3. On the middle record the message reads “Source Network Address: 10.0.4.11.” and on the oldest it also reads “10.0.4.11.” — which is exactly the chain from card 13, now confirmed a third time from a completely different direction.

Three independent views of the same fact agreeing is what evidence is. When you write your report, you can say the chain was confirmed from the summary column, from the field statistics, and from the individual records.

Next — this is the turn in the investigation

You have proved the account arrived on three servers. You still have no evidence of how it travelled. “One account, three logons” on its own is suspicious; “one account, three logons, each from the previous machine” is strong. The next step makes it provable — and it is in the other data view.

Change of view14

Switch to the network data view

126 documents1 min
Goal of this step

Move from who logged on where to what connection carried them. Logons tell you the destination. Only the network pile can tell you the route.

Do this

  1. Click the Data view dropdown on the far left of the search bar. It currently reads auth-*.
  2. Click network-* in the list.
  3. Watch the sidebar. It changes completely.

What is in this pile, and what is not

FieldIn auth-*?In network-*?What it is for
user.nameYesNoWhich account — the network pile does not know
host.nameYesYesWhich machine the record was collected on
source.ipYesYesWhere the connection came from
destination.ipNoYesWhere it went. This is the one that matters next.
destination.portNoYes3389 means RDP
network.protocolNoYesrdp, smb, dns and so on

Notice what this means for your report: the network records have no account name on them at all. You will have to join the two piles by IP address. That is normal, that is what an investigation actually looks like, and doing that join carefully on the next card is the skill being tested.

Two things to expect, so they do not worry you
  • Your columns came with you. The table still shows host.name, source.ip and host.ip from card 13, so the toolbar says Columns 4. Expected — Kibana remembers. You will add two more in a moment.
  • The old query does not apply. The card 10 query mentions event.code and user.name, and this pile has no user.name at all. Clear the search bar before you type the next one, or you will get zero results and blame the wrong thing.
If you picked All logs by accident

You will see a mixture of both piles, the counts will be neither 294 nor 126, and every number in the rest of this guide will be wrong in a way that is hard to spot. Go back to the dropdown and choose network-* explicitly. If the tab says something other than 126 with no query at all, you are on the wrong pile.

Next

Now the query that proves the movement. It is two clauses long, and both of them are about the same port.

Prove it15

Query 6 — the two RDP connections that carried it

6 of 7 queriesthis is the proof
Goal of this step

Prove the how. The logons told you where the account ended up. Only the connection records can show that it was actively carried there, and by what.

Do this

  1. Clear the search bar completely and type the query below. Press Enter.
  2. Read the tab. Then add three columns: hover source.ip, destination.ip and destination.port in the sidebar and click ⊕ on each.
Query 6 — data view network-* network.protocol: "rdp" and destination.port: 3389

What you should see

With the three columns added, the whole chain is on one screen:

And the plain-English sentence on each one

As on card 14, every record carries a message field. Click the ⇅ button on either row and you find the whole hop written out in a sentence:

The message field on the two RDP records, verbatimRDP connection established from 10.0.4.11 to 10.0.4.12:3389 (remote desktop). RDP connection established from 10.0.4.12 to 10.0.4.13:3389 (remote desktop).

Two records, two sentences, two hops. Quote one of these in your evidence section. It says in plain words what four columns of numbers say between them, and nobody can misread it.

Put the two hops next to the three logons

Time (UTC)EventFrom → ToNotes
10:00:00.000logon 4624→ 10.0.4.11 sec-win-03the foothold
10:05:00.000RDP 338910.0.4.11 → 10.0.4.125 minutes after the foothold, 2 before the next logon
10:07:00.137logon 462410.0.4.11 → landed on 10.0.4.12 sec-win-02and note where it came from: 10.0.4.11
10:14:00.000RDP 338910.0.4.12 → 10.0.4.137 minutes later, 2 before the next logon
10:16:00.274logon 462410.0.4.12 → landed on 10.0.4.13 sec-win-05and from: 10.0.4.12

Read the To column downwards: 10.0.4.12, then 10.0.4.13. Read the landed on entries downwards: 10.0.4.12, then 10.0.4.13. They are the same two addresses.

The case is now closed

Each RDP connection is aimed at exactly the address the account's next logon lands on, and each one happens two minutes before it. That is not a coincidence and it is not a similarity — it is the same event seen from two systems:

  • The network pile says: 10.0.4.11 opened a Remote Desktop session to 10.0.4.12.
  • The auth pile says: seven minutes after the first logon, somebody presented rneuman to 10.0.4.12 from 10.0.4.11, and was let in.
Finding 3 — the finding that turns an alert into a verdictExactly two RDP connections (TCP 3389) exist in the day's network telemetry. Both are internal, both are minutes apart, and each one's destination is the address of the account's next successful logon. The logons therefore form a single chain: sec-win-03 -> sec-win-02 -> sec-win-05.

And the set of targets, confirmed a second way

Click destination.ip in the sidebar to open its Top values panel:

Next

One question left, and it is the one that separates a finding from a coincidence: is this rare? If the whole network generates hundreds of RDP connections a day, two of them means nothing. Check.

Prove it16

Query 7 — is this signal, or just noise?

7 of 7 queriesthe reality check
Goal of this step

Put the finding in proportion. “Two RDP connections” is only impressive if two is not normal for this network. This card makes sure you can say so with a number instead of a feeling.

Do this — three searches, about a minute

  1. Search for destination.port: 3389. Note the count.
  2. Search for network.protocol: "rdp". Note the count.
  3. Clear the box completely and press Enter to see the total for the pile.

The three numbers, side by side

SearchDocumentsWhat it tells you
destination.port: 33892Two connections to the RDP port
network.protocol: "rdp"2Two connections the protocol field calls RDP
both together2They are the same two records. Nothing on 3389 is mislabelled, and nothing labelled rdp is on another port.
no query at all126Everything in the pile

2 out of 126 is 1.6% of the day's connections. This network does not normally speak RDP at all. Two records is not a busy protocol being misread — it is the whole of the RDP activity that exists.

Why this card is worth more than it looks

An analyst who writes “RDP traffic was observed between internal hosts” has proved nothing at all — that sentence could describe almost any network on earth.

An analyst who writes “in 126 connection records covering a ten-hour window, exactly two used TCP 3389, both internal, each aimed at the address of the next logon by the account under investigation” has proved something. Same two records. Enormously different sentence. That difference is the job.

What to do if the two numbers disagree

If destination.port: 3389 gives 2 and network.protocol: "rdp" gives 0, or one of them gives you no results and no error, then that field is stored as text instead of a number, and your numeric comparison matched nothing at all. This is not a bug you have to live with — it is exactly what the index template installed by the setup file prevents. Silent zero results are the most dangerous thing in a log tool, which is why every step in this guide tells you the number to expect.

You now have everything

Three logons, three servers, two RDP hops between them, all internal, all inside sixteen minutes, and the RDP activity is unique in the day’s traffic. That is a complete, defensible finding.

Two cards from now you will write it up. First, put the five events in order — a timeline is the heart of an incident report and it is the easiest thing to get wrong.

Put it together17

Build the timeline — the heart of the report

oldest first5 min

You have proved three separate claims. An investigator, or a manager, or a court, will not read three claims — they will read one story in time order. Assemble it now, before you write a word of prose.

Do this

  1. Open a text file, a note, or the bottom of a piece of paper.
  2. Write five lines, oldest at the top, one line per event, with its timestamp.
  3. Write the gap after each one, in minutes.

The five events, interleaved from two different data views

  • 10:00:00.000
    Logon — rneuman successfully authenticated on sec-win-03 (10.0.4.11), from 10.0.4.11. auth-*
    The foothold. Nothing in the data explains how the account got here.
  • 10:05:00.000  (+5 min)
    RDP connection — 10.0.4.11 → 10.0.4.12 on TCP 3389, event.outcome: success. network-*
    The first hop. Note it happens after the logon on 10.0.4.11 and before the logon on 10.0.4.12.
  • 10:07:00.137  (+2 min)
    Logon — rneuman successfully authenticated on sec-win-02 (10.0.4.12), from 10.0.4.11 — the machine used on the line above. auth-*
  • 10:14:00.000  (+7 min)
    RDP connection — 10.0.4.12 → 10.0.4.13 on TCP 3389. network-*
  • 10:16:00.274  (+2 min)
    Logon — rneuman successfully authenticated on sec-win-05 (10.0.4.13), from 10.0.4.12 — the machine used on the line above. auth-*
Read your own five lines and you should see this shape

logon → RDP → logon → RDP → logon. Alternating. Every connection is followed by a logon, two minutes later, on the machine it pointed at. And every logon is preceded by a connection, seven and five minutes earlier, from the machine the account was last on.

Total elapsed time: 16 minutes and 274 milliseconds. Two hops. Three servers. One account. No external address anywhere.

Two things to get right in the timeline, and one to leave out

1. Read your times off your own screen. If your machine is not on UTC, your five timestamps will all be shifted by your offset — and they will be shifted consistently, so the gaps, the ordering and the two-minute pattern are all still exactly right. Write a one-line note at the top of your timeline saying which timezone you read them in. An analyst who quietly mixes two timezones produces a timeline that is internally contradictory and cannot be defended.

2. Do not invent a sixth event. It is very tempting to add a line like “09:5x — attacker compromises credentials” to make the story start neatly. There is no evidence for it. Leave the gap, and put “initial access not covered by available telemetry” in the timeline. A timeline with a documented gap is trustworthy; one with a comfortable guess is not.

3. Do not add the noise either. The 41 failed logons, the 30 lockouts and the 22 Kerberos failures from card 9 do not belong on this timeline. They are context, and context goes in a different section. A timeline should contain only the events that advance the story.

Why the two-minute gap is worth noticing

An RDP connection at 10:05 and a logon at 10:07 is the shape of a deliberate action: open the session, then log in two minutes later. A coincidence would not line up twice, in the same order, with the same interval. The regularity is the evidence. Say so in the report — it turns five observations into a described technique, which is what a detection engineer needs to write a rule against.

The one-line version, for the top of your report
Summary lineOn 22 September 2026 between 10:00 and 10:16 UTC the internal account rneuman logged on successfully to three internal servers (sec-win-03 10.0.4.11 -> sec-win-02 10.0.4.12 -> sec-win-05 10.0.4.13), each hop carried by an internal RDP connection on TCP 3389. No external source address was involved. Assessed as a TRUE POSITIVE: compromised-credential lateral movement inside 10.0.4.0/24.

Every number in that paragraph came from a card in this guide, and every one of them is a number you can reproduce on screen. That is what makes a report defensible.

Timeline done. Now write the report around it.

Deliverable18

Write the report, then prove it

this is what is assessed25 min

Nobody reads your screen. This card is the deliverable — it is the thing you hand in, and it is the only place in the guide you type. It has two parts and both go into your submission: Part one is your written report, Part two is the set of figures you checked off your own screen as you went. Neither part has an answer printed next to it. Fill both in, then press EXPORT MY SUBMISSION at the bottom: a finished PDF report lands in your Downloads folder with your name and batch number on the front of it.

Do this yourself, and do it now

If you cannot fill a line in without going back to Kibana, you have not finished the investigation — which is exactly the point. These fields are deliberately empty and stay that way until you type. Nothing here is marked against a model answer; it is marked on whether you found these things.

Both of these are printed at the top of the exported PDF and go into the file name, so the submission is identifiable without you having to say who you are in the report itself. Leave either one blank and the file still exports — it just says [not answered] where your name should be, which is a good reason not to leave them blank.

Part one — your report

1. Summary

What happened

two or three sentences a manager could follow: what, who, how many machines, and the verdict in the first line. No jargon in that first sentence

2. Timeline

When

one line per stage, oldest first, with the times read off your own screen — not off this guide. Five stages, and the two RDP hops are part of the timeline, not a footnote. Add a line saying which timezone you read them in, and a line saying that initial access is not covered by the telemetry

3. Evidence

How you know

each query you ran, the number it returned, and what that number proved — ruled in or ruled out. The number matters as much as the reasoning, and a query with no conclusion attached to it scores nothing

4. Verdict

True positive or false positive

state it plainly in the first line, then the whole chain in one paragraph. Use the words lateral movement and compromised credential — they are the language the discipline uses. Then add what your data cannot tell you; that sentence is worth more than the paragraph before it

5. Recommendations

What should happen next

concrete actions in the order you would carry them out. Each one needs a scope and an owner. “Monitor closely” is not an action

Every line below is a number you should be able to point at on your own screen. These travel with your report, so a figure that contradicts your writing gives you away — if Part one and Part two disagree, one of them is wrong, and you want to know which before you hand it in.

Your verdict in one line

Two things worth double-checking in your own report

These are the two that catch people out, so read yours back now:

  1. Did you join the two data views by address? The logons alone are suspicious; the logons plus the two RDP records pointing at the addresses of the next two logons are the finding. A report that stops at “three logons on three servers” has described the shape of the attack without proving it. Say explicitly that you joined source.ip in the auth pile to destination.ip in the network pile.
  2. Did you state the edge of your evidence? The first logon’s source.ip equals its own host.ip, so this data does not show the initial compromise. A report that says so is trusted; a report that quietly invents a credential-theft event to tidy the start of the story is not, and that is the single most reliable way to tell the two apart.

And one bonus: if you noticed that the source ports run consecutively from 40000, or that the account did nothing else at all on the estate that day, say so in your report. Neither is required, and nothing checks it automatically, but those are the sentences that turn a list of counts into a story.

  • Part one and Part two agree. Where they differ, find out which is wrong first.
  • Your summary would still make sense to someone who has never heard of RDP.
  • Your timeline is oldest first, five events, and every line has a time on it.

Tear the lab down

leave no trace1 min

Finished. Now remove the lab completely. This matters: the lab stores its data in a Docker volume, and volumes are not removed when you close a window or shut down your computer. Left behind, it silently occupies disk space until someone deletes it by hand.

Do this

  1. Open the lab folder again.
  2. On Windows: find teardown.cmd and double-click it. On macOS or Linux: run ./teardown.sh in a terminal in this folder.
  3. It lists exactly what it is about to delete, then asks you to confirm. Nothing else is touched either way.
  4. Press Y and Enter (Windows) or y and Enter (macOS / Linux). That is the whole process.

What it deletes — and what it does not

Every one of those names begins with this lab’s own folder name, rdp-lateral-001. That is not a coincidence — it is how the script guarantees it can only ever delete its own lab, and nothing else on your machine.

What it deliberately keeps
  • The Elasticsearch and Kibana images. These are the big downloads — about four gigabytes. Keeping them means the next time you run this lab, the setup file starts in seconds instead of twenty minutes.
  • Everything else on your computer. Other Docker projects, other labs, your images, your other volumes — all untouched. The script never runs docker system prune and never removes an image.

Running it twice is also safe. The second run reports each object as not there, nothing to do and changes nothing — there is nothing left to change.

What you should see

The last thing the teardown file prints Removing... compose down -v completed Verifying... gone container rdp-lateral-001-elasticsearch gone container rdp-lateral-001-kibana gone volume rdp-lateral-001_esdata gone file .../rdp-lateral-001/docker-compose.yml gone folder .../elklab-rdp-lateral-001 ============================================================== The "rdp-lateral-001" lab has been removed.
Want to check it really worked?

Every line above says gone, and the script re-checks each object after deleting it rather than assuming. If any line says WARNING, something survived: start Docker and run the teardown file again. You can also look under Volumes in Docker Desktop, or run docker volume ls, and there should be no rdp-lateral-001_esdata entry.

Why bother?

Practical: a lab volume is real disk space, and a machine with a dozen abandoned lab volumes will eventually run out of room or fail to start new containers. Cleaning up is part of being a professional.

Discipline: an analyst who leaves environments running on a shared or corporate machine causes real problems — port conflicts, someone else’s lab failing to start, resources nobody knows are being used. Leave it as you found it is a habit worth forming now, before anyone is paying you for it.

Running it again later?

Just start the setup file again — setup-lab.cmd on Windows, ./setup-lab.sh on macOS or Linux. It rebuilds everything from scratch, and because the images are still on your machine it will be ready in a couple of minutes. The two pairs of files are designed to be used together: setup to begin, teardown to finish.

Reference⚙

If something goes wrong

keep this open

Almost every problem in this lab is one of four things. Check them in this order before assuming the worst.

A query returns nothing, or the wrong number

  • Check the time range. This is the cause nine times out of ten. It should read Sep 22, 2026 @ 08:04:34.437 – Sep 22, 2026 @ 17:59:07.708, and with no query at all auth-* must read 294. Reloading the page resets it to the last 15 minutes and the blue Search entire time range button comes back.
  • Check the data view is the one the card asks for — auth-* or network-*, and not All logs. With no query, auth-* is 294 and network-* is 126; anything else means the wrong pile.
  • Check the quotes and the field type. user.name: "rneuman" needs the quotes; event.code: 4624 must not have them (though it will tolerate them). A value in the wrong format gives you zero results and no error message at all, which is the most confusing failure mode in the whole tool.
  • Check you are on the tab you think you are. Documents ( n ) and Field statistics look similar; the count in the tab name is the same either way.

The numbers are bigger than the guide says

  • More than 294 on auth-* with no query? The data was loaded twice. Run the teardown file, then the setup file — that is clean and guaranteed to fix it.
  • Exactly double (588)? Same cause, and the confirmation: duplicates always double a count.
  • Fewer than 294? Your time range has clipped part of the day. Press Search entire time range again, or pin a wider window as card 7 describes.

The sidebar says “Empty fields” or “Available fields 0”

  • This is not a broken data view. It means “this data view has 15 fields, but none of them hold data inside the time range you have selected”.
  • Widen the range (card 7) and Available fields will replace Empty fields, and the field names will appear.
  • Only if Empty fields shows 0 as well is something actually wrong — then re-run the setup file, which verifies each data view and reads the stored index pattern back instead of printing a hopeful message.

A control I told you not to press did something

  • You pressed Try ES|QL (or Switch to classic). The search bar has been replaced by a box reading FROM auth-* | LIMIT 10. Nothing is broken — press the browser’s Back button, or press Switch to classic to return to the KQL bar. You do not need ES|QL for this lab.
  • You clicked a table row and nothing happened. Correct behaviour. Clicking the row does nothing at all. The control is the small ⇅ button in its own column immediately left of the @timestamp.
  • You clicked the eye-looking icon on a field and a panel opened off to the right. That is the Top values panel, and on cards 9 and 16 it is exactly what you were asked to open. It closes with the small × or Esc.

Elasticsearch or Kibana will not start

  • Is Docker Desktop running? It must be, and it must say Engine running. This is the cause almost every time.
  • Ports. Elasticsearch wants 9200, Kibana wants 5601. If another program already owns either, stop it — or edit the ESPORT and KBPORT lines at the top of the setup file and run it with regen-compose, which rewrites the compose file for you.
  • It refuses to start because port 9200 belongs to another cluster. That message means something else is using the port. It tells you the other cluster’s name so you can decide what to do. Nothing was changed.
  • Be patient. A cold start that downloads roughly four gigabytes and then shows nothing for several minutes is normal, not hung. The script prints a dot for every attempt and dumps the last 40 log lines if it ever gives up.
  • Do not install your own Elasticsearch or Kibana. You do not need them; the lab starts its own copies inside Docker.

Your screen does not look like the picture

  • Compare the words, not the pixels. These are real screenshots taken at 1440×900, so on a smaller window everything is scaled down and on a larger one scaled up. Every button, tab and field name in them is a real label from a real screen — if the words match, you are in the right place.
  • Your clock times are different. That is your timezone, not an error. See the box on card 7.
  • Your range is a different window. Also fine. Any window that still contains all 294 documents gives the same findings.
  • Kibana remembers where you were. If a dropdown looks odd, reload with F5 and then press Search entire time range again.
  • Stuck in a panel you cannot leave? Press Esc.
Still stuck?

Write down exactly what you clicked, what you expected, and what happened instead, then ask your instructor. That description is the skill — being able to report a problem precisely is most of a real analyst’s job.

Help

Moving around

→Next card ←Previous card HomeFirst card EndLast card ?This help EscClose this

On a phone, swipe the card left or right. On a desktop, you can also click the pills under the header to jump anywhere.

If you get lost

The row of pills under the header is your table of contents — every step, in order. The blue one is where you are.

How to use the screen pictures

They are real screenshots of this exact lab, not drawings, and they contain the answers on purpose. Hold yours next to them: if the words match, you are on the right screen and you typed the right query. The numbered circles (1 like that) point at the control to use.

They are not a substitute for doing it. The thing being assessed is the report you write from what you see.

Saving or printing

The printer button at the top right turns this whole guide into a single PDF with every card in order. The Copy button on each dark query box puts that query on your clipboard so you can paste it straight into Kibana. On the Write it up card there is a second, louder button — EXPORT MY SUBMISSION — which turns everything you have typed on that card into one finished PDF report in your Downloads folder.

The coloured markings

Yellow marks a value you have to read off your own screen and record yourself — the blank in your report. Green marks a value this guide is handing you outright: it appears in the Finding boxes from card 12 onwards and in the prose examples on the report card, and nowhere before that. On the last card you type into empty boxes instead — nothing is filled in for you there.

Stuck on a step?

Almost every problem in this lab has one of four causes, and all four are covered on the If something goes wrong card near the end: the data view is wrong, the time range reset, you are on the Alerts page with the wrong time range, or Docker is not running. Go there rather than guessing.
